FOREWORD This Indian Standard was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Hydrometry Sectional Committee had been approved by the Water Resources Divisi on Council. Some of the techniques available for discharge measurement on smaller rivers and under normal flow conditions may not be appropriate for large rivers and the hazards associated with flows during flood . These techniques may need certain modifications, if used. The choice of methodology will , in a general sense, be dictated by river dimensions, flow conditions, feasibility of measurements, measuring insrrurnents/equipments, purpose and available funds. In specific instances the choice of technique will be decided by the physical conditions at the site . Hazards discu ssed in this standard are confined to those peculiar to the measurement of discharge in large rivers and floods .

In the formulation of this standard, considerable assistance has been derived from ISO 9825 : 1994 'Measurement of liquid flow in open channels - Field measurement of discharge in large rivers and floods', issued by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO).
For rhe purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value. observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in accordance with IS 2 : 1960 'Rules for rounding off numerical value s (revisedi' . The number of significant places ret ained in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard.

Indian Standard
MEASUREMENT OF LIQUID FLOW IN OPEN CHANNELS - FIELD MEASUREMENT OF DISCHARGE IN LARGE RIVERS AND FLOODS
1 SCOPE
This standard deals specifically with the measurement of discharge in large rivers and the measurement of flows during floods. It also describes the relevant field measurements when it becomes necessary to use indirect methods of estimating discharge.

3 DEFINITIONS
For the purpose of this standard. the following definitions in addition to those given in IS 1191 shall apply. 3.1 Large River - River which presents measurement problems because of its large discharge or large physical parameters. 3.2 Flows During Flood - High discharge corresponding to or exceeding natural bankful stage; an unusually high discharge associated with high stage.

4 UNITS OF MEASUREMENT
The units of measurement used are SI units.

5 APPROPRIATE TECHNIQUES
Due to the dimensions of large rivers and the hazards associated with flows during floods. some of the

IS 15772: 2008
techniques available for discharge measure~ent on smaller rivers and under normal flow conditions may not be appropriate or may need modification, if used. The choice of methodology will, in general, be dictated by river dimensions, flow conditions, feasibility of measurements, measuring instruments and equipment, purpose and availability of funds. In specific instances the choice of technique will be decided by the physical conditions at the site. Hazards discussed in this standard are confined to those peculiar to the measurement of discharge in large rivers and floods. These techniques which may be partially or entirely appropriate within certain limitations imposed by the degree of difficulty of operation are: a) Velocity-area methods (see IS I 192) I) Current meters, and 2) Floats. capable of measuring wide range of velocities need to be used in such ca ses . If none of these possibilities exist, a measurement having higher uncertainty may have to be accepted .

6.3 Logistic Problems
The basic problems in the measurement of discharg e in large rivers and during floods are logistics, associated either with the time required for measurement or with the need for special resource s to be employed. However, flood mea surement may al so be accompanied by significant additional hazard to personnel and equipment. An additional logistic problem is access to the flood measurement site, both in being able to reach the site and getting to the site in time to measure high flows . Because of this, indirect measurements assume great importance in case of tloods.

b) Tracer dilution methods [see IS 9163 (Part 1)] c) Weirs and flumes (see IS 6330, IS 9108, IS 12752, IS 13083, IS 13084, IS 14574, IS 14673, IS 14869, IS 14974 and IS 15353). d) Indirect methods [see IS 1191, IS 2912, IS 15119 (Part I), IS 15119 (Part 2)] I) in situ measurement, and 2) remote sensing methods

7 MEASUREMENT OF DISCHARGE IN LARGE RIVERS 7.1 Problems of Scale
The problems relating to measurement of discharge in large rivers are essentially those of scale.

7.1.1 Large Width
For most methods large width presents difficulties in ascertaining the location of the measurement point with respect to the cross-section, since the conventional means using tag-lines and optical survey instruments, depending upon the actual dimensions, may result in higher uncertainty. More sophisticated position -fixing equipment may be needed to overcome this problem (see IS 15352) .

6 NATURE OF DIFFICULTIES LIKELY TO BE ENCOUNTERED AND POSSIBLE SOLUTIONS 6.1 Difficulties Likely to be Encountered in Measurement or Flow Parameters
When any of the three parameters used to determine discharge (width. depth and velocity) is abnormally large, it may involve difficulties. Large width may pose problems for position-fixing in the horizontal, and for measurement of velocity in any over bank spill portion. Large depth may create difficulty in locating a measuring device at the desired depth. High velocities cause problems with regard to maintaining station. position-tixing and location of measurements in both the horizontal and vertical. These difficulties are accentuated by problems caused by floating debri s, high turbulence and vortices, flash floods. movement of large bed forms , etc.

7.1.2 Large Depth
Large depth may call for a greater number of points on the vertical to be measured to sample mean velocity, particularly if the vertical velocity distribution is not uniform due to the section being non-uniform. When using current meters, wet-line distortions lead to timeconsuming corrections and even then the measurement point may well deviate from the cross-sectional line with which it is meant to conform.

7.1.3 High Velocity
In many cases high velocity creates difficulties both with regard to locating a measuring platform at the desired position on the horizontal and in maintaining that position. as well as enabling the desired point on the vertical to be sampled. The turbulence, which usually accompanies high velocity, compounds the problems of sampling and reduces the accuracy of measurement. 2

6.2 Possible Solutions
It may become necessary to change data collection processing techniques to allow for the effects of the diffi.c~lties discussed in 6.1. which may then require additional field measurements. The current meter

7.2 Velocity-Area Method (Using Current Meter)
The most suita ble meth od for meas uring the discharge of large rive rs is the veloci ty-a rea method usin g a current meter, fro m a power boat or motor launch fitted with an echo-sounder or from a bridge. During high floods. fixing of po sition and othe r param eters may be made by ca bleway with a trolley for rivers up to 500 m wide. From 500 m up to I krn width, a boat may be moved across the river with the hel p of a cableway, For river widths gre ater than I krn, the use of cablew ays is exclud ed. Stationary boa ts ancho red with great ca re ca n be used for po sit ion -fixin g for river s having width up to 2 km. The care required in such oper ation s, co upled with the need for adequate verticals to be measured, inevitably result s in a single total mea surement becoming a very lengthy procedure. This can be partially reduced by the use of several teams with severa l boats and current meters. Measurements obt ain ed by differ ent teams would need to be integrated ove r the cross-section. Simil arl y, ad va nc e notice of likel y ri ver- st ag e behaviour enables me asurem en ts to be plann ed to take ad vantage of stable stag e condition s, to counter the problem oflengthy measuring period s. Significant river traffic may cause further delay. The moving-boat technique is the most suitable method of tackling the problem, since the time element is then reduced to manageable proportion s. Nevertheless. the probl em of tracking the boat be comes greater with increasing river width. The fixed depth of the current meter pre sent s problems of cal ibration , if the river sec tion varie s in depth. It may become necessary to define a number of un iform sec tions, each of which mu st be cal ibrated by a statio na ry bo at at vary ing stages. cl imatically host ile environment, it has proved possible to drop dyes from airborne pla tform s into selected river reache s, by sequential air photos to ob serve the time of travel, and thu s estimate the flow ve loci ty. Thi s velocity with the cros s-sectional area is then used to compute the d ischarge. The method requires survey knowled ge of the sec tional area through the reach.

7.3.3 Structures
Th e large d imen sions invol ved imply that structures are unlikel y to be available. Th is again is a que stion of sca le . If, howe ver, a barrage exis ts it sho uld be co nsidered for the measurement of flow.
NOTE - A bar rage is a gated weir for regulat ing flows; the gates are ope ned during flood period s.

7.3.4/ndirect Methods
Indi rect meth ods such as the slope-are a method or the contracted-opening method, may be used on large rivers in situa tions where other methods of measuring di sch arge ca nnot be used .

8 MEASURE MENT OF FLOWS DURING FLOODS UP TO BANKFUL STAGE
8.1 Problems 8.1.1 The d ifficulti es ass ociated with the measurement of flows during floods, although in some cases of a natur e similar to tho se encounte red in measuring large river flows, differ in one critic al respect; namely, tha t flo ws during floods are often as sociated w ith c ircumst ances which cause add itional ha zards in respect of the safe ty of personnel and equ ipment. As s uc h thi s requires trained a nd experienced crew memb ers and ob servers. Flow s du ring floods may also exh ibit rapidly ch anging conditions in which timing may be critical and difficult to judge. In add ition the rate of change in stage may be crit ical. High velocity creates difficulties in measuring flows during floods and flows in large rivers (see 7.1.3) . Measuring the direction of the current relative to the section ca n be both difficult and uncertain. However, this problem can be reduced to a certain extent by the use of a direction -reading current meter. 8,1.2 A permanent gauging station used under normal river condition s may not be appropriate for measuring with in -b ank flows during flood s and it may be nece ssary to se lec t a more appropriate site for the mea surement of flow s during flood . 8.1.3 Rivers in flood tend to carry varying amounts of debris picked up by the swollen waters. Such debri s. coupled with high veloci ty and turbulence of currents, often make s the use of boats too hazardous. and even cableways and bridges may not be usable as platforms

7.3 Other Methods
The remaining techniques tend to be less appropriate and less accurate.Iargely because of various difficulties due to the width of the river.

7.3.1 Floats
Floats in general fall into this category. However, by stationing ob servation boats across the ob servation sect ions at some convenient interval, it might be poss ible in some measure to overcome this diffi cult y. The increase in logistic and procedural problems might be considered tolerable if co st precludes moving-boat and stationary-boat techniques.

7.3.1. Tracer Dilution Techniques
Tracer dilution techniques in general, also appear to be less appropriate for the same reason. However, in special circumstances including remoteness and

for current meters because of the damage likely to occur to the meters and suspension cables. Howe ver, up to certain limit s, which depend on the individual river , it should be possible to obtain at least surface velocity measurements from cableways and bridges. The mean velocity may be assessed if, during normal stage measurements, the relationship between surface velocity and me an ve loc it y has already been demonstrated and continues to hold good at the flood stage. Though these short-cut methods will produce representat ive discharge for the me an stage during the measurement. there will be higher uncertainty. extensive scouring and filling , thereby affecting the shape and ch a rac teristics of the river cross-section during measurement, the moving-boat technique may be used. However, consequent ch ang es in the vertical velocity curves may require correct ions to the velo city coefficients.

8.4 Optical Velocity Meter
If it is not poss ible to conduct discharge me asurements at the sec tion line, an echo-sounder may be used for establishing the cross-section at the bridge or barrage site, and by measuring the velo city of the flows during floods under the bridge or barr age with an optical velocity meter it is feasible to assess flows during floods with a reasonable degree of accuracy. However, suitable equipment is required to keep the transducer horizontal at the time of depth measurement. A slant-line optical current meter may be used for measurement of velocity and the discharge calculated with a previous survey of the cross-section, if scouring or siltatio n is low or absent.

8.2 Use of Floats
In unavoidable circumstances floats and the use of floating debris for measuring surface velocity in unavoidable circumstances provide a means of reducing the hazard in respect of safety of personnel and equipment. Preparations for flood mea surement by these means should be made during normal stages with a survey of the reach selected and soundings of the section s to be used . The team of observers should be trained with a full awareness of their duties. The difficulties which relate to the usc of floats lie in the tracking of the floats through the stretch so that the accurate length of flow path will be known , and the positioning of the floats into trajectories, which will adequately sample the whole width of river. The first of these difficulties impl ies the use of conventional survey equipment by experienced operators, while the second implies the use of some kind of catapult equipment to lob the floats into the river so that they fall at varying ranges across the river. If a bridge is conveniently located, the float s may be dropped from the bridge at the desired distances from the bank . As with all surface velocity measurements, corrections are necessary to est imate mean velocities. Weighted floats may also be used to eliminate the necessity for calibration. However, it is desirable to check the accu racy of the weighted float by carrying out periodic calibrations. Weighted floats with longer lengths (up to 5 m) are made so that they float vertically and give more or less average velocities (integral of verti cal velocity distribution over the float length, which may be more or less equal to the depth of flow). In flows during floods up to bankful stage, the depth of flow will be high and weighted floats may not normally be feasible. in particular because flow depth is required to be nearly uniform along the stretch.

8.5 Barrages
Where structures such as barrages exist in the river, they can be used for estimation of the discharge based on surveys of the high-water marks and the geometry of the structure. In the case of a barrage, the flow s during floods can be measured with a good degree of accuracy by observing gate openings and the upstream and downstream water levels.

8.6 Tracer Dilution Methods
Tracer dilution methods require a coordinated effort, and suitable access for both injection and sampling is necessary. They require large amounts of chemicals which may be difficult to handle conveniently and if radioactive tracers are used safety precautions must be strictly followed [see IS 9163 (Pan I)]. Moreover the mixing lengths are likely to be very large, with Intermediate inflows or spills. However, in the case of mountain torrents in flood, the dilution method may . be the only method suitable.

8.7 Indirect Methods 8.7.1 In the absence of direct measurements, indirect
determinations of discharge after the passage of a flood may be the only way to assess the flow . Such methods make use of the energy equation for computing stream flow. The specific equations differ for different types of flow, but they all involve the following general factors: a) Physical characteristics of the channel, that is dimensions and shape of the channel within the reach, and boundary conditions;

The over bank flow and/or standing water can then be measured by curre nt meter and sound ing. The ultrasonic method may also be used to good advantage in measuring over bank flow, but the moving -boat technique is not recommended.
